"an outlet called WCC tech claiming the series X is as powerful as this GPU"

I did not make any claims equating FP32 performance to overall performance either. Merely, it is just an example where they stated the 4090 far exceeds that of the Xbox's performance, in one metric.

Now, there is an argument for equivalent performance. Since a developer can better optimize for a fixed hardware configuration. To some extent, PC gaming leaves performance on the floor in order to stay generic to the various hardware configurations that can exist. Think SIMD instruction extensions for CPUs, but you can't use them if you have to support a minimum generation CPU that doesn't have it, as one example. Or the infamous shader compilation, which is drastically simplified on consoles (the exact GPU hardware and driver version is known). 

So, to summarize. I still have found no evidence of the original claim. However, I did search as I would find it quite funny to see such a claim. So, if they did make such a claim, please guide me in the direction for my own amusement.

Joule as an energy unit is usually taken for physical energy, like 1 joule is the energy needed to lift a 100 gram apple 1m high. Or as a unit to measure the power of projectiles.
Watt as a performance unit is usually used, when comparing engines or electrical devices.
Using joules to measure the performance of an electrical device like a video card absolutely makes no sense, even though it is possible. That beeing said: you lost me at 4:05 when measuring the performance per watts not in watts but joules per frame. author: @novocainDaimon

text: @novocainDaimon  I can't explain why no one else may or may not do something, but from first principles alone it is fine to use Joules for a per frame energy consumption value. You can't use Watts for that because Watts don't tell you an amount, it tells you how fast energy is flowing. They do actually use Watts as part of the calculation here and it is in their chart. But when you do the math, the units cancel out such that time is no longer relevant. 1 Watt = 1 Joule per second. So, if you account for FPS (frames per second), then you can easily get Joules from the measurement of Watts (power) the card was pulling in that moment.

In the past I've been called a fanboy for pointing out these embarrassingly unprofessional and cunning stances taken by Richard Leadbetter towards AMD: I am a tech and PC enthusiast with 20+ years of experience, I use all the brands of hardware/software, all of them, I use what serves me the best; when I look for reviews and analyses, I expect the reviewer to be neutral and fair towards all the brands that compete against each other in the review, because that's ultimately the most important aspect for consumers who want to take informed decisions when buying products. This guy systematically skews all of that, giving us a very partial and biased view.

My point is that the entire world computing industry has mostly been increasing efficiency by the transistor shrinking, for the past 60 years... however, the the entire world computing industry is running into the physical limitations of silicon itself. Meaning, yes, alternatives could come in. Yet, no alternatives are fully solved yet, and even when they are, transitioning to a completely different paradigm is not a trivial matter. Hence, we will see some improvements in the near future (1-5 years), but the main driver of the performance improvements was the transistor shrinking with silicon, which is reaching the end of its capabilities. text: I think it should be noted that DLSS3 isn't quite just adding a "few ms" of input lag and massively improving performance. It's adding that extra few ms vs the base framerate but vs the framerate it's targeting, it's significantly laggier. So for instance a 30FPS game frame generated to 60 will still feel like a bit worse than the same game at 30FPS input latency wise, and while it'd look like 60FPS it won't play like 60FPS. Ofcourse the higher the framerate the lower the impact of it as the differential narrows down.

text: I think in DLSS 3 you are gaining performing. Gaming performance is not a matter of pushing the game state over a wire in some recondite way. Gaming performance is about displaying the game state visually in a way that is interpreted well by the brain. And, particularly on a sample-and-hold display, increasing frames per second allows the brain to interpret the visuals better as real motion and less as some hack trying to fool the brain. People are worried about the inaccuracy of the generated frames, and rightly so. But I think most don't stop to consider that the entire experience is inaccurate because using still images to represent motion is itself a hack that has inherent inaccuracies. Increasing frame time reduces those inaccuracies, since the information that is trying to be delivered is not the frames, but rather the continuous-time 3-dimensional game world. It's entirely possible for the overall understanding of the scene to be improved by greater frame rates even if some of the individual frames are less accurate because they are AI generated.

text:
It didn't quite stagnate yet, but for me, it still looks like a game of being between a rock and a hard place:
-they'll run out of die shrinks eventually, and in fact, effective die size for lower end GPUs has been increasing even taking into account node shrinks: GTX 1060 (200mm^2, TSMC 16nm); RTX 2060 (445mm^2, TSMC 14nm); RTX 3060 (276mm^2, Samsung 8nm, which is a die size reduction compared to the RTX 2060, but still an increase compared to the 1060 despite going from TSMC's 16nm to Samsung's 8nm); RTX 4060...

-Bigger dies mean more power hungry chips, and Nvidia have been able to stick with 250w max for top GPUs pretty much until the RTX 2000 series, but that was no longer the case with the RTX 3000 series and onwards, with all the implications associated (ATX3.0 and PCIe 5.0 connectors to handle the power increase)

-Silicon wafer sizes and dies sizes have physical limits from a production pov (silicon wafers are currently 300mm in diameter, and reticle limit allows for die sizes of ~800mm^2 max), as well as economical limits from a production pov (how much will a RTX 6060 with a +500mm^2  die size cost?) 

-There's only so much performance gains a new GPU architecture can do at any given node shrink

The good news is that what's already out there should be enough for quite a few years, but something will have to radically change eventually...

DLSS 3.0 will have graphical artifacts like any frame interpolation technique. Doesn't matter how much AI power you throw at it. Motion interpolation always will suffer from artifacts and increased latency. Motion interpolation is an algorithm that has to estimate a next fake frame based on the previous frame. Hence the increased latency. After that comes a real frame which might and will collide in some cases with the previous fake frame. Hence the artifacts. No matter how much you'll tweak this algorithm it will never be perfect and is nothing more than a version found on any TV from the last 10 years. Usually these motion interpolation techniques on your TV's are called motion interpolation, motion smoothing, motion flow etc.

author: @chengcao418

text:
@chengcao418  Well, no, that's not the whole story. 

Power curves aren't linear in GPUs. In fact, there are reports out there now that embargos are up that the 4090 is a bit overcranked and can drop double digit percentages on load for single digit performance drops, which could make it even more efficient running against a fps cap than it is running unlimited on some games. 

Joules per frame is a meaningless stat that has little real world application. Different games will have very different results, capped and uncapped performance will yield different numbers and different cards may relate differently under different scenarios or with different tuning of the card. 

I mean, it's fine to make the point that the 4090 has a disproportionate performance boost compared to its increase in power draw, but in this case it's much more meaningful to know that the power draw is in line with the 3090 most of the time, and it's even more interesting to know it's factory overclocked and its optimal performance point would have been to cap its maximum power draw on par with it as well.
author: @mademedothis424

text: @mademedothis424  true, if you want to look at capped frame rate performance at the minimum required power then power curve will change the dynamics here. However if the performance is uncapped, Jules per frame is the exact same metric as power consumption. However why would you want to spend more money for the same performance? The power consumption savings here isn't worth the money you just payed
